subject: What a Terraform backend is
description: A backend defines where Terraform stores its state data files. The docs state: 'The backend defines where Terraform stores its state data files.' Backends allow state to be centrally stored so multiple team members can access and collaborate on the same infrastructure, rather than each person holding a local state file.

subject: Purpose of Terraform state
description: State's primary purpose is to store bindings between objects in a remote system and resource instances declared in configuration. Terraform uses state to determine what changes to make, and does a refresh prior to any operation to update state with real infrastructure. State also improves performance for large infrastructures by avoiding a full rescan on every operation. [AUDIT: source (developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/state) supports the bindings claim and the refresh-before-operation claim verbatim, but does not state 'by avoiding a full rescan on every operation' as the performance mechanism -- that clause is an unsourced rationale (Prohibition 2).]

subject: Backend configuration syntax and partial configuration
description: A configuration can only provide one backend block, and a backend block cannot refer to named values like input variables, locals, or data source attributes. You do not need to specify every required argument in the backend block itself - missing values can be supplied via a config file with -backend-config=PATH, command-line key/value pairs with -backend-config="KEY=VALUE", or interactive prompts during init. This is the mechanism teams use to keep per-environment backend settings out of shared configuration.

subject: Automatic state locking on write operations
description: State locking happens automatically on all operations that could write state, with no message shown when it succeeds. If state locking fails, Terraform does not continue. Not all backends support locking, so the guarantee is backend-dependent. Most commands support a -lock=false flag to disable locking, which the docs advise against using.

subject: force-unlock and the lock-ID nonce
description: When automatic unlocking fails, terraform force-unlock provides manual recovery, but the docs warn: 'Be very careful with this command. If you unlock the state when someone else is holding the lock it could cause multiple writers.' The command requires a unique lock ID that Terraform outputs only when unlocking fails, functioning as a nonce that ensures locks and unlocks target the correct lock rather than any lock.

subject: terraform plan computation steps
description: terraform plan performs three sequential operations: it reads the current state of already-existing remote objects to make sure state is up to date, compares the current configuration to the prior state noting differences, then proposes a set of change actions that would make remote objects match configuration. Plan alone does not carry out the proposed changes - it is a preview for review before apply.

subject: Speculative plan staleness before apply
description: When using speculative plans (not saved to a file), the docs warn: 'other changes made to the target system in the meantime might cause the final effect of a configuration change to be different than what an earlier speculative plan indicated, so you should always re-check the final non-speculative plan before applying.' This is a stated limitation of plan review in team/CI workflows where time elapses between plan and apply. [AUDIT viable->wounded: Stage 2 merged T-036 into this row and appended a claim -- 'both recommend committing to one saved plan file rather than re-planning at apply time' -- that this row's own source (developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan) never states; that page's advice is to re-check the final plan, not to freeze one. T-036's source makes the opposite-facing recommendation (apply exactly the saved file, no re-planning). These are two distinct, source-grounded claims in real tension with each other -- the tension itself is a real team-scale plan/apply discipline question -- so the merge was incorrect and has been reversed; T-036 is restored to viable as its own row. See T-036.]

subject: Remote state sharing via terraform_remote_state
description: With remote state, Terraform writes state data to a remote data store shared between all team members, eliminating the need for each user to manually ensure they have the latest state and that nobody else is running Terraform simultaneously. The terraform_remote_state data source lets teams share output values read-only across configurations, allowing infrastructure to be decomposed into smaller, independently-managed components.

subject: CLI workspaces: state-per-workspace mechanics
description: The persistent data in a backend belongs to a workspace; a backend initially has only one workspace ('default', which cannot be deleted) containing one state. Multiple workspaces let you deploy distinct instances of the same configuration without configuring a new backend or changing credentials. Terraform does not access resources in other workspaces when you switch - they still physically exist but are invisible until you switch back.

subject: Workspaces vs. directories for environment separation
description: HashiCorp explicitly states CLI workspaces are not appropriate when organizations want strong separation between deployment stages (e.g. staging/production) that need different credentials and access controls, because 'CLI workspaces within a working directory use the same backend, so they are not a suitable isolation mechanism for this scenario.' The recommended alternative is separate configurations (directories) that each instantiate reusable modules against a different backend, so each environment gets its own backend config and credentials.

subject: Module tree should stay flat
description: HashiCorp's module composition guidance: 'In most cases we strongly recommend keeping the module tree flat, with only one level of child modules,' assembling reusable building blocks by composition rather than deep nesting.

subject: Dependency inversion in module composition
description: Modules should receive their dependencies from the root module (via input variables) rather than creating or looking up their own dependencies internally. This lets the same module be recombined for different results, since dependencies could later come from resources, data sources, or elsewhere without changing the module itself.

subject: Preconditions to encode module assumptions/guarantees
description: Modules carry implicit assumptions and guarantees. HashiCorp recommends using configuration validation with preconditions to make these explicit, so maintainers and consumers of the module can see the design intent rather than inferring it.

subject: Data-only modules
description: Modules need not always create infrastructure - they can encapsulate data retrieval from existing systems (data sources only), which is useful for sharing common infrastructure information consistently across multiple subsystems without duplicating lookup logic.

subject: Module scoping: encapsulation, privilege, volatility
description: HashiCorp's three module-scoping principles from enterprise engagements: encapsulation ('Group infrastructure that is always deployed together'); privileges ('Restrict modules to privilege boundaries' - resources needing different permission levels should not coexist in one module, to avoid accidental segregation-of-duties violations); and volatility ('Separate long-lived infrastructure from short-lived' - pairing stable resources like databases with frequently-changing ones like app servers introduces unnecessary risk). [AUDIT: all three principles (encapsulation/privileges/volatility) are verbatim-correct, but 'from enterprise engagements' is not stated on the cited page -- unsourced provenance attached to a correctly-quoted rule (Prohibition 2).]

subject: Module nesting depth and external module compatibility
description: The tutorial advises: 'Generally, do not nest primary modules more than two deep,' with an exception for simple utility modules. It further warns that externally-sourced nested modules risk unexpected breakage, so 'revisions to external modules should be backwards compatible.'

subject: Module MVP principle (80% use cases, maximize outputs)
description: The tutorial recommends: 'Always aim to deliver a module that works for at least 80% of use cases,' avoiding excess conditional logic and exposing only commonly-modified arguments as variables initially. It also recommends outputting 'as much information as possible from your module MVP even if you do not currently have a use for it,' to enable downstream module composition later.

subject: OIDC token exchange mechanics for dynamic credentials
description: The dynamic credentials flow: (1) HCP Terraform generates an OIDC-compliant workload identity token containing info about the organization, workspace/Stack, and run stage; (2) the token is sent to the cloud platform with auth details; (3) the cloud platform verifies the token using HCP Terraform's public signing key; (4) on success, the platform returns fresh temporary credentials; (5) these are configured in the run environment; (6) the plan or apply executes; (7) the run environment is torn down and credentials discarded. Self-hosted agents require v1.7.0+ to support this.

subject: CI pipeline: separate plan/apply steps and plan-file portability constraints
description: HashiCorp's automation tutorial recommends running init, plan, and apply as distinct steps (terraform init -input=false; terraform plan -out=tfplan -input=false; terraform apply -input=false tfplan). After plan, the entire working directory including .terraform must be archived and made available to the apply step, and both steps must run on the identical absolute path, operating system, and CPU architecture, since 'Terraform assumes that the plan will be applied on the same operating system and CPU architecture as where it was created.'

subject: CI credential handling and PR secret exposure risk
description: The tutorial recommends using environment variables for provider authentication credentials rather than persisting them to disk, since env vars 'are not included in the plan or persisted to disk by Terraform in any other way.' It separately warns that 'passing sensitive/secret data to Terraform via variables or via environment variables will make it possible for anyone who can submit a PR to discover those values' in pull-request-triggered plan workflows.

subject: VCS-driven speculative plans for PR review
description: As part of HashiCorp's recommended collaboration workflow, HCP Terraform's VCS integration generates speculative plans for each pull request, showing the exact changes Terraform will make, so teams can review infrastructure changes before they are merged/applied. This is presented as the review layer that sits above remote state and locking in the progression toward team collaboration. [AUDIT: the speculative-plan claim is verbatim-supported, but the closing sentence ('the review layer that sits above remote state and locking in a progression') is the harvester's framing, not the source's -- the page lists remote state, code review, and CI/CD as parallel practices, not a layered progression (Prohibition 2).]

subject: Multi-account/environment split strategy
description: For teams scaling Terraform usage, HashiCorp suggests splitting managed resources into multiple accounts in a way that makes organizational sense, giving the example of 'an account per deployment environment,' as one strategy alongside single-cloud, hybrid, or multi-cloud boundaries.

subject: Health assessments / automated drift detection mechanics
description: HCP Terraform health assessments run periodic, non-actionable refresh-only Terraform plans in configured workspaces to compare real infrastructure against the state file. A health assessment never interrupts or interferes with runs - if a new run starts during an assessment, the assessment cancels and reschedules. Requirements: Terraform 0.15.4+ for drift detection alone (1.3.0+ for drift plus continuous validation), remote or agent execution mode, and the workspace's latest run must have been successful. Available only in Standard and Premium HCP Terraform editions.

subject: Configuration drift vs. state drift distinction
description: HCP Terraform's docs draw an explicit distinction: 'Configuration drift differs from state drift. Drift detection does not detect state drift.' Configuration drift is a mismatch between real infrastructure and the Terraform configuration; state drift involves external changes that don't necessarily invalidate configuration. When configuration drift is found, HCP Terraform proposes the changes needed to bring infrastructure back in sync with configuration.

subject: Policy-as-code position in the plan/apply pipeline
description: In HCP Terraform, for each run in selected workspaces, the platform checks the Terraform plan against the configured policy set - policy evaluation happens during planning, before apply. Depending on enforcement level, failed policies can stop the run. Users with appropriate permissions can override failed policies. HashiCorp recommends storing policies in version control for 'standardization, security, and auditability.' [AUDIT depth judgment->operation: the depth_check as harvested justified judgment by pointing at a decision ('choosing enforcement levels and who may override') the row's own content does not actually teach.]

subject: Dependency graph: node types and 9-phase construction
description: Terraform builds a dependency graph and uses it to perform operations like generating plans and refreshing state. The graph contains resource nodes (one per instance when count is used), provider configuration nodes, and resource meta-nodes (convenience groupings for count>1 that don't represent actions). Construction proceeds through 9 phases: add resource nodes with diff/state metadata; link resources to provisioners; add explicit depends_on edges; incorporate orphaned resources present in state but not configuration; connect resources to provider config nodes; parse interpolations for implicit dependencies from resource-attribute references; add a root node pointing to all resources; split destroy/create nodes when diffs exist (since destroy order often differs from create order); and validate no cycles exist and there is a single root.

subject: Dependency graph: depth-first parallel execution, default concurrency 10
description: Terraform walks the dependency graph via a standard depth-first traversal, but with parallelism: 'a node is walked as soon as all of its dependencies are walked,' enabling concurrent operations while respecting dependency constraints. The default concurrency limit is 10 simultaneous nodes, adjustable via the -parallelism flag on plan, apply, and destroy. The docs describe changing it as 'an advanced operation' that 'should not be necessary for normal usage.'

subject: State locking and force-unlock
description: Terraform locks state automatically before any write operation; if state locking fails, Terraform does not continue. Teams hit this when a CI runner is killed mid-apply (OOM, timeout, spot termination) or someone Ctrl+C's a long-running apply, leaving a stale lock. The trap is reaching for `terraform force-unlock` without first confirming no other process actually holds the lock: HashiCorp's own docs warn 'Be very careful with this command. If you unlock the state when someone else is holding the lock it could cause multiple writers,' and specify force-unlock is meant only to clear your own lock after automatic unlocking failed.

subject: CLI workspace selection before apply
description: A team running environments as Terraform CLI workspaces had an engineer apply without checking which workspace was selected; production instances scaled down to the dev instance count (2 instead of 20), a production incident lasting 15 minutes and affecting 200+ users. The practitioner attributes this to workspaces making the active environment implicit - the same command applies to whichever workspace is currently selected, with no directory-level signal of which environment is being touched.

subject: Choosing Terraform CLI workspaces vs. directory-per-environment
description: A practitioner who migrated a team from CLI workspaces to per-environment directories reports the workspace setup accumulated conditionals keyed on `terraform.workspace` (e.g. `contains(["prod","staging","staging-eu","staging-special"], terraform.workspace)`) that became hard to audit, and that after migrating to folders 'code reviews went from mental workspace simulation to reading 50 lines of actual config,' with no further wrong-environment incidents. Their stated default is per-environment folders for teams under 25 engineers and up to 12 environments, prioritizing explicit configuration over the DRY-ness of workspaces. [Stage 2: considered as a possible duplicate of T-010 (harvest-canon, 'Workspaces vs. directories for environment separation') - same subject and same depth, but not merged: T-010's claim is HashiCorp's stated reason (credential/access-control separation), while this row's claim is a practitioner's distinct reasons (unauditable per-workspace conditionals, code-review cost) plus a concrete team-size/environment-count threshold not present in T-010. Kept as two rows carrying different supporting evidence for a related recommendation.]

subject: Backend state key collisions across environments
description: Copying a dev directory to stand up staging without updating the backend's state key left both environments writing to the same state file. Applying staging caused Terraform to diff staging's desired config against the shared state (which reflected prod), and it began reconciling by modifying prod resources to match staging's configuration. Recovery took about 4 hours: using CloudTrail to determine which resources belonged to which environment, manually importing them into separate state files, then re-applying to correct drift.

subject: Single state file per team instead of per service
description: One team's state file grew to roughly 15,000 lines managing 200+ resources. Renaming a module in that shared state nearly triggered destruction of an 85-resource production AKS cluster, because the blast radius of any single state operation covered everything in the file. The source frames the fix as one state file per service per environment - more initial overhead, but far safer to operate. [AUDIT viable->wounded: two of three claims misattributed. The source's '85 resources' is the blast radius of the whole monolithic state (which happened to include the production AKS cluster among other resources), not '85-resource production AKS cluster' as the row states. The row also states 'the source frames the fix as one state file per service per environment'; the source instead recommends splitting by lifecycle, blast radius, and team ownership (5-8 state files for medium infrastructure), not per-service-per-environment granularity. The headline trap (monolithic state = full blast radius on any operation) and the '15,000 lines / 200+ resources' figures are verbatim-supported.]

subject: terraform destroy confirmed in the wrong context
description: A junior engineer ran terraform destroy and typed 'yes' to confirm while in the wrong context, deleting 11 production resources including virtual networks and managed disks before the process was halted. The source notes state versioning and resource locks limited the damage but did not prevent it. [AUDIT viable->wounded: the mitigation clause misattributes cause. Source: 'What saved us: 1. Azure Soft Delete ... 2. Azure Resource Locks on the most critical resources -- Terraform's destroy failed on those with a CanNotDelete lock error' -- these are Azure platform features on the cloud resources, not Terraform state versioning or Terraform state locking as the row implies. Neither Terraform mechanism was involved, and state locking would not have prevented a correctly-locked destroy from running. Minor: source describes a single VNet and 3 managed disks; row pluralizes to 'virtual networks and managed disks'. The core incident (destroy confirmed in the wrong context, 11 resources deleted) is supported.]

subject: Unmanaged out-of-band changes silently reverted by later applies
description: A support engineer manually upgraded a database SKU outside Terraform. Weeks later, an unrelated apply reverted the database back to the SKU still recorded in Terraform's state, affecting production - because Terraform's state, not the live resource, is its source of truth, and nothing had reconciled the two in between. [AUDIT viable->wounded: the row's causal mechanism is wrong and contradicts T-002/T-006 in the same file. The row claims the revert happened 'because Terraform's state, not the live resource, is its source of truth' -- but Terraform refreshes state from live infrastructure before planning (the source itself says 'Terraform saw the drift'). The revert happened because the CONFIGURATION still declared the old SKU, and apply converges toward configuration; state is the binding record, not the desired-state source of truth. As written the row teaches the reader the opposite of how plan/apply actually works. The incident itself (manual SKU change reverted by a later unrelated apply) is supported.]

subject: Running apply without a pre-generated plan file
description: Running terraform apply directly, without first saving and applying a specific plan file, lets Terraform generate a new plan at apply time, which can differ from whatever was reviewed, because time passes between review and execution during which real infrastructure or configuration may change. The described discipline is to plan to a file, review that exact plan, then apply that file rather than re-planning at apply time. [Stage 2: merged into T-007 (harvest-canon, 'Speculative plan staleness before apply') as a duplicate - same subject (plan/apply time-gap risk) and same depth (judgment); both recommend committing to one saved plan file and re-checking it rather than letting apply re-plan.] [AUDIT merged->viable (restored): Stage 2 incorrectly merged this row into T-007 as a duplicate. T-007's source says to re-check the final non-speculative plan before applying; this row's source says a saved plan file is applied exactly, with no re-planning. Different sources, near-opposite prescriptions -- not a duplicate. Restored to viable.]

subject: count versus for_each for resource collections
description: When resources are created from a list using the count meta-argument, removing an element from the middle of that list shifts the index of every subsequent element. Because count tracks resources in state by index number, this causes Terraform to plan changes to (and can destroy/recreate) resources that were never actually modified. for_each avoids this because it tracks resources by a consistent key rather than position, so removing one element only affects that element's resource. HashiCorp's own help-center article demonstrates this with a plan comparison: for_each destroys only the removed item, count modifies several and destroys one.

subject: Refactoring resource/module addresses without a moved block
description: By default, Terraform interprets a changed resource or module address (e.g. from a rename) as an instruction to destroy the existing object and create a new one at the new address, per HashiCorp's own docs. A moved block tells Terraform the existing state should follow the address change instead, avoiding the destroy/recreate. The docs also warn that removing a previously-added moved block later is itself a breaking change, since any config still pointing at the old address will then plan to delete rather than move: HashiCorp recommends retaining historical moved blocks to preserve the upgrade path for module users.

subject: Assuming Terraform detects drift automatically
description: A long-time Terraform user's GitHub issue lists 'no in-built, pull-based, GitOps friendly, automatic drift detection and synchronisation' as a core operational gap: detecting drift requires manually running terraform plan (or -refresh-only), and 'automated reconciliation via cron jobs is unreliable' when configuration is complex. Terraform does not watch infrastructure and flag changes on its own - someone or something has to run a plan for drift to surface at all. [AUDIT viable->wounded: the second quoted phrase is not a quotation. The row presents "automated reconciliation via cron jobs is unreliable" in quotation marks as source text; the GitHub issue (hashicorp/terraform#31736) instead says 'You cannot reliably implement a cron job, because a lot of times an automatic Terraform apply can fail.' A paraphrase presented as a quotation, with a substituted rationale ('when configuration is complex' vs. the source's 'an automatic Terraform apply can fail'). The first quoted phrase ('no in-built, pull-based, GitOps friendly, automatic drift detection and synchronisation') is verbatim-correct and the headline claim stands.]

subject: Treating a clean plan as a guarantee the apply will succeed
description: The same practitioner GitHub issue states: 'You assume that if you do a terraform apply, it will work. But more often than not, when you actually do the terraform apply, it errors out' - because a plan is computed against the provider's current view of things, and by apply time, provider-side state, quotas, or dependent resources can have changed, or the provider API can reject a change the plan predicted would succeed.

subject: Choosing OIDC over static long-lived credentials for CI/CD
description: A walkthrough of wiring GitHub Actions to AWS for Terraform notes that with static AWS access keys stored as CI secrets, 'anyone with access to the CI/CD logs can easily use the echo command and retrieve them,' that such keys 'needed to be rotated frequently - ideally weekly or monthly - to limit the window of compromise,' and that even with rotation they 'remained active between deployments, increasing the risk of misuse.' OIDC instead issues temporary, scoped credentials that 'automatically expire once the workflow is complete' and are bound to the specific workflow run, removing the standing-access window static keys create. [Stage 2: absorbs T-018 (harvest-canon, 'Why dynamic provider credentials over static') as a duplicate - see T-018 for the merge reasoning.]

subject: Building a reusable local module
description: Official HashiCorp tutorial: 'Build and use a local module.' Walks through creating a module directory with main.tf/variables.tf/outputs.tf that provisions a public S3 static-website bucket, declaring input variables (bucket_name, tags), exposing outputs (ARN, name, domain), running terraform get to install the local module, then calling it from a root configuration and applying. Frames the underlying practice as treating every configuration as a potential module for reuse.

subject: Detecting and reconciling drift with -refresh-only and import
description: Official HashiCorp tutorial: 'Manage resource drift.' Provisions an EC2 instance, key pair, and security group with Terraform, then intentionally introduces drift by modifying the security group via the AWS CLI outside Terraform. Detects the change with terraform plan -refresh-only, applies the refresh to sync state without touching infrastructure, imports a manually-created security group into management, then runs terraform apply to reconcile configuration and infrastructure, verifying with SSH/HTTP checks.

subject: Automating Terraform plan/apply with GitHub Actions
description: Official HashiCorp tutorial: 'Automate Terraform with GitHub Actions.' Sets up an HCP Terraform team token, workspace, and a template GitHub repo, then builds a plan workflow that runs on pull requests (uploads a speculative/read-only plan and comments the output on the PR) and an apply workflow that runs on pushes to main. Uses a stored HCP Terraform API token (TF_API_TOKEN, a GitHub Actions secret) for authentication rather than OIDC - useful as a plan-on-PR/apply-on-merge review-discipline exercise, but not an OIDC example.

subject: Configuring OIDC-based dynamic provider credentials
description: Official HashiCorp tutorial: 'Authenticate providers with dynamic credentials.' Walks through setting up a trust relationship between HCP Terraform and a cloud provider via OIDC, running Terraform locally to establish the provider-specific trust configuration, setting workspace variables to enable dynamic credential requests, then provisioning infrastructure through HCP Terraform using the established trust. Covers AWS, GCP, Azure, and Vault, plus AWS EKS and GKE variants.

subject: Setting up S3 remote state with DynamoDB locking, then migrating
description: Official HashiCorp tutorial: 'Migrate state from S3 to HCP Terraform.' Has the reader create an S3 bucket and DynamoDB table for state storage and locking, deploy an EC2 instance against that backend, create CLI workspaces (default and dev), then replace the S3 backend configuration with HCP Terraform's cloud block, rename workspaces, assign a variable set with AWS credentials to the new workspaces, and run plan/apply remotely through HCP Terraform before cleaning up.

subject: HashiCorp Certified: Terraform Associate sample questions
description: Official HashiCorp sample-questions page for the Terraform Associate (004) certification. Provides real example questions in the exam's three formats (true/false, multiple choice, multiple answer) covering topics including state file contents (e.g. that secrets referenced as variables end up in plain text in state), variable map syntax, automatic loading of terraform.tfvars, which commands refresh state, and what happens during apply. States explicitly: 'The exam questions are not intended to trick you.'

subject: Drill: state locking and plan/apply staleness
description: Stand up a shared backend (S3+DynamoDB, or HCP Terraform) with two local checkouts simulating two team members. From checkout A, start a long apply against a resource with a deliberate delay (e.g. a null_resource with a sleep provisioner) so the lock is held. From checkout B, attempt a second apply and observe the lock error (T-004). Kill checkout A's process mid-apply to leave a stale lock, then decide - and write down your reasoning before running the command - whether it is safe to `terraform force-unlock` using the lock ID Terraform reports, given what you can and cannot verify about whether A's process is truly dead (T-005, T-029). Separately, generate and save a plan file, let five minutes pass while manually changing a tagged resource outside Terraform, then apply the saved file and observe that it applies the stale plan rather than current reality - demonstrating why the docs say to always re-check the final plan (T-007). [AUDIT viable->wounded: the closing segment inverts the distinction it cites. It has the reader save a plan file, let a resource change out of band, then apply the saved file and 'observe that it applies the stale plan rather than current reality -- demonstrating why the docs say to always re-check the final plan (T-007)'. T-007's warning is specifically about SPECULATIVE plans (not saved to a file); applying a saved plan file is the opposite case T-036 covers (apply exactly what's in the file, no re-planning). The predicted observation is also unreliable, since a saved plan is lineage/serial-checked against state and is likelier to error than silently apply stale. The locking half of the drill (T-004/T-005/T-029) is sound.]

subject: Drill: module design refactor (encapsulation, privilege, volatility)
description: Take a single, unscoped Terraform module that provisions a VPC, an RDS database, and an autoscaling app-server group together (deliberately violating T-015's principles). Refactor it into separately-scoped modules following encapsulation/privilege/volatility (T-015), apply dependency inversion (T-012) so the database module receives its VPC ID as an input rather than looking it up itself, add at least one precondition (T-013) encoding an assumption the original module left implicit, and cap nesting depth per T-011/T-016. Then write one sentence on what would have broken later - not immediately - had you shipped the original monolithic version to a second team.

subject: Drill: CI/CD credential hardening (static keys to OIDC)
description: Build a minimal GitHub Actions workflow that plans and applies Terraform against a real or sandbox cloud account using a static access key stored as a repo secret. Confirm you can retrieve it from the Action's own logs with an `echo` step (per T-041's cited risk), then delete that step and the static key, and rewire the workflow to use OIDC/dynamic provider credentials (following the pattern in T-045, HashiCorp's dynamic-credentials tutorial) so the workflow requests short-lived, run-scoped credentials instead. Confirm no long-lived secret remains in the repo's secret store when you're done. [AUDIT viable->wounded: the drill instructs an observation the platform prevents. GitHub Actions automatically masks registered repository secrets in workflow logs, so a plain 'echo' of the secret prints '***', not the value -- a reader following the drill literally will wrongly conclude the exposure risk doesn't exist. T-041's underlying claim (re-verified this turn) is correct; only this drill's demonstration step is broken.]

subject: Drill: workspaces-vs-directories migration
description: Build a two-environment (dev/prod) setup using Terraform CLI workspaces against one backend, sized so that `terraform.workspace` gates at least one differing value (e.g. instance count). Deliberately reproduce T-030's failure mode: switch to the dev workspace, then run apply while believing you are targeting prod, and observe how little signal there is that you are in the wrong workspace. Then refactor into two separate directories, each with its own backend configuration and credentials, re-run the same change, and write down at what team size or environment count (compare your answer to T-031's stated threshold) you would judge the workspace approach acceptable versus not.

subject: Drill: drift detection and configuration-drift-vs-state-drift classification
description: Provision a small resource set with Terraform (e.g. a security group and an EC2 instance). Outside Terraform, make two separate changes: (1) modify a resource attribute directly via the cloud CLI (configuration drift - the live resource no longer matches your .tf files), and (2) construct a scenario where the state file alone diverges from configuration without any live change (state drift, per T-025's distinction). Run `terraform plan -refresh-only` to detect and apply the refresh for case (1), then explain in one sentence why the same command would not have caught case (2) - grounding your answer in T-025's stated distinction that 'drift detection does not detect state drift.' [AUDIT viable->wounded: case (2) teaches a definition its own cited row contradicts. The drill asks the reader to 'construct a scenario where the state file alone diverges from configuration without any live change (state drift, per T-025's distinction)' -- but T-025 and its source (HCP health-assessments docs) define state drift as external changes to real infrastructure that do not invalidate configuration, i.e. still a live change. A state file diverging from configuration with no live change is just an ordinary pending change any 'terraform plan' reports, not state drift, and is not constructible as described. Case (1) (configuration drift via cloud CLI, detected with -refresh-only) is sound and stands on its own.]

subject: The dependency lock file (.terraform.lock.hcl)
description: AUDIT DISCOVERY -- absent from the harvested/merged set; no row mentions the lock file, required_providers, or version pinning of any kind. terraform init creates and updates .terraform.lock.hcl, which 'belongs to the configuration as a whole, rather than to each separate module.' HashiCorp's instruction is explicit: 'You should include this file in your version control repository so that you can discuss potential changes to your external dependencies via code review, just as you would discuss potential changes to your configuration itself.' Once a provider selection is recorded, init reuses that exact version 'even if a newer version has become available'; terraform init -upgrade is what 'disregard[s] the existing selections and once again select[s] the newest available version matching the version constraint.' Without a committed lock file, two engineers and CI can each resolve a different provider version from the same configuration and produce three different plans from identical code -- the single most direct way a team loses plan reproducibility.

subject: The lock file does not lock module versions
description: AUDIT DISCOVERY -- absent from the harvested/merged set. The dependency lock file covers providers only. HashiCorp: 'At present, the dependency lock file tracks only provider dependencies. Terraform does not remember version selections for remote modules, and so Terraform will always select the newest available module version that meets the specified version constraints.' The trap is assuming committing .terraform.lock.hcl froze the whole dependency set. It did not: a registry module without a version constraint silently upgrades on the next init, on whichever machine inits next. The module block's version argument is the only guard, and HashiCorp recommends 'explicitly constraining the acceptable version numbers to avoid unexpected or unwanted changes' -- but that argument is available only 'when the source argument points to a module listed in a registry', so a team sourcing modules from raw Git URLs has no version argument at all and must pin via the source ref itself. This is the unstated condition underneath the module-reuse cluster (T-011 through T-017): that guidance assumes consumers can pin what they consume, and nothing else in the set says how.

subject: State stores secrets in plaintext, so state access is an access-control decision
description: AUDIT DISCOVERY -- present in the merged set only as an incidental clause inside an exam-practice row (T-047) and a passing mention of the backend `encrypt` option inside a tutorial's steps (T-046); no row states it directly. HashiCorp: 'If you are developing with Terraform locally, Terraform stores your state in a plaintext file, which includes any secret values you defined in your configuration.' Marking a variable or output sensitive obscures terminal output; it does not keep the value out of state. Recommendations are backend-dependent and explicit: 'You can encrypt your state at rest, but the encryption method depends on your specific backend'; 'The S3 backend can encrypt state at rest if you enable the encrypt option, and protects state with TLS in transit'; 'HCP Terraform automatically encrypts state at rest and protects it with TLS in transit.' Alongside: 'Use access controls to limit who has access to your state' and 'Use audit logs to track state access over time.' At team scale this converts a storage choice into a permissions decision -- read access to the state bucket is read access to every credential any provider has ever returned.

subject: Saved plan files are sensitive artifacts
description: AUDIT DISCOVERY -- absent from the harvested/merged set. The plan/apply-review cluster (T-007, T-020, T-021, T-036) tells a team to write plans to a file with -out and to archive the working directory between CI stages, and none of those rows say what the plan file contains. HashiCorp's plan documentation does: 'If your plan includes any sort of sensitive data, even if obscured in Terraform's terminal output, it will be saved in cleartext in the plan file. You should therefore treat any saved plan files as potentially-sensitive artifacts.' The automation tutorial repeats the warning for the archived working directory: 'If any of these contain sensitive data then the archived working directory containing the plan file should be protected accordingly.' The trap is the team-scale shape this takes: the recommended CI pipeline uploads that archive as a build artifact, and on most CI platforms build artifacts are readable by anyone who can read the job -- a wider audience than the state backend was ever scoped to.
